name: WireGuard
summary: A compact UDP secure tunnel implementation that maintains per-peer Noise handshake and key state, queues encryption and handshake work, and rejects replayed transport counters through a sliding window.

features.name: Per-peer Noise handshake state
features.description: WireGuard maintains a handshake object for each peer and implements the Noise_IKpsk2_25519_ChaChaPoly_BLAKE2s exchange. Initiation and response transitions update chain keys, hashes, ephemeral keys, indices, timestamps, and handshake state before deriving transport keys.
benefits: Provides authenticated key establishment with forward-secret session keys
Keeps peer identity and ephemeral handshake state separate from device-wide routing state
Makes handshake transitions and key derivation explicit in the implementation
costs: Handshake state has ordered transitions and concurrency protection requirements
Rekey timers and packet loss require retry and queue behavior
The security properties depend on correct cryptographic and timestamp handling

features.name: Bounded encryption and handshake work queues
features.description: The Go implementation separates outbound encryption, inbound decryption, and handshake queues as bounded channels with wait-group lifetime accounting. Device startup creates worker routines for encryption, packet handling, and handshake processing.
benefits: Separates cryptographic work from network and tunnel I/O
Bounds queued work and makes shutdown closure explicit
Allows multiple encryption workers while preserving per-device queue ownership
costs: Queue capacity and worker counts affect latency and memory under load
Shutdown requires all producers and consumers to coordinate with queue references
Backpressure and packet drops must be understood separately from cryptographic validity

features.name: Rotating session keypairs with replay window
features.description: After a handshake, a peer holds current, previous, and next keypair slots. Each keypair has send and receive AEAD state, a monotonically increasing send nonce, and a replay filter that accepts counters only once within a bounded sliding window and below the protocol limit.
benefits: Supports key rotation while retaining a previous receive key during transition
Rejects duplicate and stale transport packets without requiring in-order UDP delivery
Binds packet acceptance to authenticated counter state
costs: Multiple keypair generations increase transition and cleanup state
The replay window consumes per-peer memory and rejects packets outside its bound
Nonce and key lifetime limits remain protocol-critical operational constraints

mathematical_views.question: How do authenticated initiation and response messages move a peer from zeroed handshake state to a transport-key state?
assumptions: A peer handshake has explicit states for initiation creation/consumption and response creation/consumption
Each transition consumes validated message fields and updates cryptographic state
The view abstracts primitive internals while retaining key and timestamp dependencies

mathematical_views.question: How do device-wide queues and workers route tunnel packets, encryption work, and handshakes to per-peer state?
assumptions: The device is a coordinator vertex and peers are state vertices
Bounded channels represent work edges with explicit close and reference lifetimes
The graph does not infer fairness from channel order or worker scheduling

mathematical_views.question: Which authenticated transport counters are accepted, rejected as duplicates, or rejected as too old?
assumptions: Counters are checked after authenticated decryption
The receiver stores a greatest counter and a finite ring of prior bits
The relation models anti-replay acceptance and not end-to-end delivery

benefits: Small explicit state machine for authenticated rotating sessions
costs: Handshake ordering, timers, and cryptographic state require careful synchronization

benefits: Separates packet I/O from cryptographic worker execution
costs: Bounded capacity and shutdown accounting constrain overload behavior

benefits: Forward progress over unordered UDP with replay rejection
costs: Key generations, counters, and finite windows add per-peer state and limits
